title: The stronger the model, the more lethal dirty data: cleaning becomes more valuable
dek: Jane Street's alt data team finds that once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; nailing down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.
why: This episode is dense with how data engineering actually creates value; the latter half on corrections, timestamps, and cost models offers judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.
who: CTOs building data teams, quant practitioners evaluating data vendors, and engineers who believe LLMs will automatically clean data.
skip: Pure tech background can skip to the data engineering part after 33 minutes, but don't miss the negative oil price at 19 minutes.

points.h: Patterns get competed away once discovered
points.body: Eric defines this as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, patterns you find are often quickly digested by others and the market, then stop working; little knowledge accumulates like physical laws. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio in trading data is naturally poor—the market's mechanism constantly squeezes out extractable signals, leaving the rest closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you must keep finding new facts, not cling to old patterns.

points.h: Prices can go negative; don't hard-code assumptions into systems
points.body: On April 20, 2020, CME crude futures near expiry settled at a negative price—just that one day, and the final settlement later turned positive. The reason wasn't that oil was worthless, but that storage at Cushing, the delivery point, was nearly full and no one wanted physical delivery. Order and risk systems that long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion: a large part of trading is understanding the messy details of reality—storage capacity, contract multipliers, quote units—and systems that get these details right define the risk ceiling.

points.h: Domain experts don't know how good tools can be
points.body: For data and systems to be truly usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have high tolerance for painful processes, worn down by Excel and manual workflows to the point they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the real mechanics of the domain to engineers, and 'how good it can get' to traders. Every desk at Jane Street now has such an embedded developer, a role that grew out of this initial need.

A classic alt data example is counting cars in Walmart parking lots—more people in cars means better business. Eric says this example is actually bad: you want to infer spending, but spots only tell you foot traffic, quite indirect; about 20% of Walmart's shopping happens online, and cities like New York have no lots to count. More direct signals are on the transaction side: card issuers, Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spend, and can sell anonymized aggregates to buy-side firms.

points.h: Corrected data turns backtests into time machines
points.body: When deciding whether to subscribe to a dataset, the vendor may have already corrected past errors; backtesting on pretty corrected data tests not what you would have actually received at the time, but the right answer known later. Eric says that's like simulating having a time machine. Jane Street's solution: save every raw piece of data and the local timestamp of receipt, so no matter how many transformations later, you can reconstruct 'what we knew at that moment.' This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data arrival time.

points.h: LLMs know the future; keep them away from historical data
points.body: AI has two impacts on alt data: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make extracting features from text easier. But beware a causal trap—using the latest LLM to featurize old documents brings in later events: it knows Enron's eventual fate and may have seen subsequent revisions of that financial report in training data. This creates new future leakage, especially when processing historical data; you must pin down 'which model version at which point in time.'

points.h: Stronger models make data cleaning more valuable
points.body: A common expectation: as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric thinks the opposite: once models can do more themselves, you need less manual feature work, but the data fed in must be more correct. If data isn't point-in-time and leaks future info into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models have varying tolerance for outliers and dirty patches. Net, cleaning data becomes more valuable, not less.

points.h: Usage-based pricing tempts teams to nickel-and-dime
points.body: Jane Street hosts its data warehouse in its own data center, not purely out of control. Eric observes: moving the same queries to a cloud vendor priced by read volume or compute time gets so expensive you think 'that money could buy a bunch of hardware.' More importantly, the cost model distorts behavior—usage-based pricing makes teams constantly optimize bills and reshape workloads to fit billing; self-hosting turns cost into a one-time hardware investment, so teams spend time on research and queries, not saving money.
